doc.title: Evan Christopher interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 1, 2009

title: What motivates kids in New Orleans brass bands; school music programs
summary: Responding to Rowe's memory of a corner brass band, he says exposure to parades, funerals and school marching bands is the point of entry into music. Formal music programs keep being cut.

bands.name: St. Augustine High School marching band

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Getting my first drums, with or without lessons

blocks.x: When my wife and I were there it was shortly before Katrina and we got to see at least one of the corner brass bands playing. It looked to be high school-aged kids. And having witnessed it for the first time, I thought it was really neat, also the fact that they were playing, I remember them playing “Stand By Me” with this funky second line groove or something. And I just was enthralled by it. And I wondered what motivates that aged kid to do that? Do you have any idea?
What motivates them to pick up instruments?
I’m assuming that they’re carrying on a tradition. But that could be an incorrect assumption.

No, no, of course it’s a tradition. You interviewed Wendell Brunious, one of the New Orleans musicians that’s — I showed you that picture of him when he was like six or seven years old standing there with his sister watching, well I guess it was the Olympia band, oh no, it might have been the Tuxedo. His father played in the Tuxedo band. So of course it’s a tradition. But it’s evolved a little bit. The marching bands of St. Augustine High School, that’s a coveted membership in this marching band. It’s a thing of honor. They get to travel and I think they were in the Rose Bowl parade in California. The brass band tradition for a lot of these young students of New Orleans, the marching, the brass band, is really their point of reference for instrumental music and their point of entry into the experience of playing music. There’s not a lot of formal music programs in the schools. They are still being cut left and right as much as we want to be able to say yeah, we know how essential music is. Well the contradiction is that our schools, we still have principals that are cutting music programs. Even this year we lost two or three. So it’s not that New Orleans is superior because we value music more, it doesn’t work like that. But these kids have been to Mardi Gras parades and seen, by the time they’re old enough to play an instrument they’ve seen dozens of brass bands, they’ve seen dozens of marching bands, they’ve had funerals where there was a band performing for the person who died and they’ve walked behind. They’ve known musicians in their community. They know what musicians look like. So yeah, the tradition, the exposure is there. No one is thrusting instruments in their hands and saying hey check this out, like they have to do everywhere else. They’re waking up with it and they have older brothers and sisters that went to the same school. Just driving down the street, you know, kids are funny, they get out of band practice and some of them don’t put their horns back in their case, they’re still at the bus stop. They’re not making the most musical sounds but I mean they’re still beating on crap
